entries.title: Your first Python program
text: Python runs the instructions in a program. `print()` displays a value. A `#` outside a string starts a comment, which Python ignores.
entries.code:
# This comment is for a reader.
print("Hello!")
entries.pitfall: Keep paired quotes and parentheses. `print` and `Print` are different names.

entries.title: Strings and quotation marks
text: A string is text. Matching single or double quotes mark a string literal in Python. The delimiters are not displayed by `print()`.
entries.code:
print("12")
print(12)
entries.pitfall: The outputs can look the same while `"12"` is text and `12` is a number.

entries.title: Run, Test and Submit
text: Run shows what your program does. Test runs examples. Submit checks the full mission and records a pass. Your draft saves as you work; the Grimoire unlocks by completion.
entries.code: print("Ready to try!")
entries.pitfall: Run alone does not mark a lesson complete. Use Program input only for code that calls `input()`.

entries.title: Names and assignment
text: Assignment binds a name to a value. Reassigning it does not recalculate values you created earlier. Descriptive names make units and responsibilities visible.
entries.code:
minutes = 12
message = f"{minutes} min"
minutes = 20
print(message)  # 12 min
entries.pitfall: Use `=` for assignment and `==` for equality.

entries.title: Strings and cleaning text
text: Strings are text. Methods such as strip return a new string; use the returned value. `strip` removes whitespace at both ends, not spaces inside a name.
entries.code:
name = "  Radio room  "
clean = name.strip()
print(clean)  # Radio room
entries.pitfall: Calling `name.strip()` alone does not update name.

entries.title: Input and numeric conversion
text: `input()` returns text. `int` converts whole-number text and `float` converts decimal text. Conversion failures raise exceptions; robust recovery is a later topic. The workshop supplies one input answer per line in Program input.
entries.code:
count = int(" 3 ")
length = float("2.5")
print(count * length)  # 7.5
entries.pitfall: `"3" * 2` repeats text. Conversion is different from display formatting.

entries.title: Arithmetic and grouping
text: Multiplication and division bind more tightly than addition and subtraction. Parentheses group quantities. Keep units consistent before combining them.
entries.code:
per_item = 8
packing = 2
print((per_item + packing) * 3)  # 30
entries.pitfall: A one-time fee belongs outside per-item repetition.

entries.title: `True` and floor division
text: `/` preserves a fractional quotient. `//` gives a floored quotient. With non-negative integers, floor division counts complete groups. For negative values it rounds down rather than toward zero.
entries.pitfall: Do not floor a value when the remaining fraction still matters.

entries.title: Remainder and unit splitting
text: `%` gives the remainder. For non-negative amounts and a positive divisor, it is from zero to less than the divisor. Combine quotient and remainder to split units.
entries.code:
seconds = 143
print(seconds // 60)  # 2 minutes
print(seconds % 60)   # 23 seconds
entries.pitfall: Remainder and number of complete groups answer different questions.

entries.title: F-strings and decimal display
text: An f-string substitutes expressions inside braces. `:.2f` displays two decimal places, including trailing zeros. Formatting changes presentation, not the precision of the underlying calculation.
entries.code:
average = 7 / 2
print(f"Average: {average:.2f}")  # Average: 3.50
entries.pitfall: round alone does not guarantee two displayed decimal places; binary floats are not exact for every decimal.

entries.title: Comparisons and Boolean values
text: Comparisons `return True` or `False`. `<` and `>` exclude equality; `<=` and `>=` include it. `==` means equal and `!=` means not equal. Return a comparison directly when it already answers the question.
entries.code:
needed = 30
available = 30
print(needed < available)   # False
print(needed <= available)  # True
entries.pitfall: Test the exact boundary as well as values on either side. The strings `"False"` and `"True"` are text, not Boolean values.

entries.title: Choosing a branch
text: `if` tests a condition; `elif` provides another choice and `else` is the fallback. In one chain, only the first matching branch runs. Independent `if` statements are separate decisions.
entries.pitfall: Indentation decides what belongs to a branch. A zero denominator must be handled before division.

entries.title: `for` loops and `range()`
text: A `for` loop repeats its indented body for each value supplied by range. `range(stop)` starts at zero and excludes stop. `range(start, stop)` also excludes stop. An empty range performs no iterations.
entries.code:
for number in range(1, 4):
    print(number)  # 1, then 2, then 3
entries.pitfall: Use `sessions + 1` as the stop only when you intentionally need labels 1 through sessions.

entries.title: Accumulating a total
text: An accumulator holds state across loop iterations. Initialize it before the loop, update it inside, and return the final value after the loop. A zero-iteration loop leaves the initial total.
entries.code:
total = 0
for turn in range(3):
    total = total + 4
print(total)  # 12
entries.pitfall: Initializing inside the loop resets the total. Returning inside the loop ends the function early.

entries.title: Defining and calling functions
text: `def` creates a function; the body runs when you call it. Parentheses distinguish a call from referring to the function itself. The caller continues after the call when the function finishes.
entries.code:
def twice(value):
    return value * 2

result = twice(6)
print(result)  # 12
entries.pitfall: `result = twice` stores the function, not its calculated return value.

entries.title: Parameters, arguments and defaults
text: Parameters are names in a definition; arguments are values supplied by a caller. Positional arguments follow order. Keyword arguments identify the parameter by name. A default supplies a value when its argument is omitted.
entries.code:
def add_fee(amount, fee=2):
    return amount + fee

print(add_fee(10))
print(add_fee(amount=10, fee=0))
entries.pitfall: Caller variable names need not match parameter names. Mutable default values require care in a later topic; these examples use numbers.

entries.title: Return, print and `None`
text: `return` sends a value back and ends the current call. `print` displays text. A function that reaches the end without returning a value returns `None`. Store a result when you need to inspect or reuse it.
entries.code:
def add_two(number):
    return number + 2

result = add_two(5)
print(result)  # 7
entries.pitfall: Printing a number inside a helper does not return that number to its caller.

entries.title: Local scope and explicit dependencies
text: Parameters and names assigned inside a function are local to that call. Returning a value does not export local names. Python can read module names, but using explicit parameters makes changing inputs easier to trace.
entries.code:
def adjust(value):
    value = value + 3
    return value

original = 5
changed = adjust(original)
print(original)  # 5
entries.pitfall: Rebinding an integer parameter does not reassign the caller name. Mutable objects need a fuller model when we reach collections.

entries.title: Reading a traceback
text: Start at the last line for the exception type and message. Then find the nearby `mission.py` frame that points to your code. Earlier frames show which calls led there.
entries.pitfall: A failing test is evidence of a mismatch, not always an exception. Do not hide a typo by adding an unrelated outside variable.

entries.title: Indentation and blocks
text: Indentation groups statements inside a function, branch or loop. Put a colon after the block header and indent its body by four spaces. Returning to the original indentation ends the block.
entries.pitfall: The indented line belongs to the branch. The final `print()` is outside it and runs either way.

entries.title: Both conditions: `and`
text: and combines requirements that must all hold. Chained comparisons are another readable form for numeric intervals. In these examples every operand is a Boolean comparison.
entries.code:
print(3 <= 5 and 5 <= 8)
print(3 <= 5 <= 8)
entries.pitfall: `value >= low and high` does not compare value with high; write the second comparison.

entries.title: Either condition: `or`
text: `or` accepts either condition, including both. It is useful when either of two situations leads to the same decision.
entries.code:
print(False or True)  # True
print(True or True)   # True
entries.pitfall: `or` is inclusive: two true conditions still pass.

entries.title: Reverse a condition: `not`
text: not turns a true condition false and a false condition true. With well-named Boolean flags it can express a blocker naturally.
entries.code:
online = True
blocked = False
ready = online and not blocked
entries.pitfall: Do not confuse negating one flag with negating an entire grouped condition.

entries.title: Guard clauses and early return
text: A `return` ends the current call, including when it occurs inside an `if` or loop. Guard clauses handle special cases before the main calculation.
entries.pitfall: A `return` inside a loop ends the entire function, not just the current iteration.

entries.title: Normalize text and compare whole choices
text: `strip` removes surrounding whitespace and lower normalizes letter case. Both return new strings. String membership checks substrings; list membership will check complete elements.
entries.code:
command = "  STOP  ".strip().lower()
print(command == "stop")  # True
print("st" in command)   # True
entries.pitfall: A substring is not a complete command. Do not let an empty string or partial word pass a whole-command contract.

entries.title: While loops and termination
text: `while` checks its condition before each iteration. It may run zero times. Update the state so the condition eventually becomes false, or exit deliberately with `break`.
entries.pitfall: A forgotten update can create an infinite loop. Syntaxia Stop terminates the worker without discarding the draft.

entries.title: `break` versus `return`
text: `break` exits the nearest loop and execution continues after it. `return` exits the current function. In nested loops, break affects only the inner loop it belongs to.
entries.pitfall: Breaking a loop is not the same as ending a function or stopping all surrounding loops.

entries.title: Skip an iteration: `continue`
text: `continue` moves to the next iteration of the nearest loop. It is useful for filtering without deep nesting. In a `while` loop, ensure necessary state updates are not accidentally skipped.
entries.pitfall: `continue` does not end the loop. A skipped while-loop update can prevent termination.

entries.title: Nested loops and grids
text: An inner loop runs for each outer iteration. Two range loops can visit every coordinate of a rectangle. Keep whole-grid accumulators outside both loops.
entries.pitfall: A `return` inside the inner loop ends the function before most coordinates are visited.

entries.title: Command loops and persistent in-memory state
text: A command loop repeatedly accepts an action. Initialize session state before the loop. Consume only the input required by that action. The state lasts while the process runs; it is not saved to disk.
entries.pitfall: Forgetting which commands read extra lines shifts every later input. Workshop Program input is a finite prepared stream, not a live terminal.

entries.title: Lists, length and indexes
text: Lists are ordered and mutable. `len(items)` gives their length, and `items[0]` reads the first element. Indexes refer to positions, not values. Lists may be empty.
entries.code:
devices = ["Radio", "Printer"]
print(len(devices))
print(devices[0])
entries.pitfall: A list of length n has last positive index `n - 1`. Accessing an absent index raises `IndexError`.

entries.title: Negative list indexes
text: Negative indexes count backward. `-1` means the last element and `-len(items)` means the first when the list is nonempty.
entries.code:
letters = ["A", "B", "C"]
print(letters[-1])  # C
entries.pitfall: An empty list still has no last element; a negative index can also be out of range.

entries.title: List slices
text: `items[start:stop]` includes start and excludes stop. Missing bounds mean the beginning or end. A slice creates a new outer list and tolerates bounds beyond its length.
entries.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(numbers[1:3])
print(numbers[:2])
entries.pitfall: Indexing returns an element; slicing returns a list. A shallow slice does not recursively copy nested objects.

entries.title: Mutating a list with `append`
text: List mutation changes an existing object. `append` adds one element at the end and returns `None`. Different names can refer to that same mutable object.
entries.code:
items = ["A"]
other = items
items.append("B")
print(other)  # ['A', 'B']
entries.pitfall: Do not assign the result of `append()` back to the list name.

entries.title: Removing and returning an element
text: `list.pop()` removes and returns the last element. `list.pop(index)` selects another position. It mutates the list and raises `IndexError` when the index is absent.
entries.code:
queue = ["A", "B"]
job = queue.pop()
print(job, queue)
entries.pitfall: `pop` returns an element, not the remaining list. Check the empty case when the contract permits it.

entries.title: Iterate and filter list values
text: `for item in items` visits each value in order. Build a new output list to filter without changing the collection being traversed.
entries.pitfall: Removing elements from the list being iterated can shift positions and skip work.

entries.title: Position and value with `enumerate`
text: `enumerate(items)` yields index/value pairs. A loop can unpack each pair into two names. Use `start=1` for human-facing numbering while remembering actual list indexes still begin at zero.
entries.code:
for number, label in enumerate(["A", "B"], start=1):
    print(number, label)
entries.pitfall: The display number is not necessarily a valid list index when `start=1`.

entries.title: Membership in strings and lists
text: in has a collection-specific meaning. A string contains substrings; a list contains elements that compare equal. `not in` negates membership.
entries.code:
print("a" in "cat")      # True
print("a" in ["cat"])    # False
print("cat" in ["cat"])  # True
entries.pitfall: Whole-command choices should not accidentally use substring matching.

entries.title: Sorting with and without mutation
text: `sorted` returns a new list. `list.sort` changes that list and returns `None`. Both keep duplicate values. Numeric sorting compares numbers; textual sorting follows string ordering.
entries.code:
values = [3, 1, 2]
new_values = sorted(values)
print(values, new_values)
entries.pitfall: Assigning `values = values.sort()` loses the local list reference by assigning `None`.

entries.title: Copies, aliases and shared objects
text: Assignment shares an object reference. copy or a full slice produces a separate outer list. Shallow copies still share nested objects, so they are enough for these flat strings and numbers but not every future structure.
entries.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
c = a.copy()
b.append(3)
print(a)  # [1, 2, 3]
print(c)  # [1, 2]
entries.pitfall: Do not treat rebinding a name and mutating a shared object as the same operation.

entries.title: Simple list comprehensions
text: `[expression for item in items]` builds a list from a transformation. An optional if condition filters items. Use this for a compact, readable operation, not to compress every multi-step loop.
entries.code:
values = [-1, 2, 3]
positive_squares = [value * value for value in values if value > 0]
entries.pitfall: A comprehension creates a new list; it should not be used just to hide side effects.

entries.title: Dictionary records and key lookup
text: A dictionary maps keys to values. Use braces for a literal and square brackets with a key for required lookup. Insertion order is preserved in Python dictionaries.
entries.code:
device = {"name": "Radio", "quantity": 2}
print(device["name"])
entries.pitfall: A missing required key raises `KeyError`. Dictionaries use keys rather than list positions.

entries.title: Optional lookup with `get`
text: get retrieves a dictionary value with a fallback for a missing key. It does not mutate the dictionary. An existing value of zero, `False` or `None` is still an existing value.
entries.pitfall: get does not insert its default. Do not confuse a false-like stored value with an absent key.

entries.title: Add and update dictionary entries
text: `mapping[key] = value` changes the supplied dictionary in place. It inserts a missing key or replaces an existing value. Replacing an existing key does not move its position.
entries.pitfall: Assigning `mapping = {...}` only rebinds the local name; it does not update the caller's original mapping.

entries.title: Dictionary key presence
text: `key in mapping` checks keys. It is independent of the associated value. Use membership when you need to distinguish absent keys from keys with `None` or zero.
entries.pitfall: `for value in mapping` iterates keys by default, not values.

entries.title: Dictionary value views
text: `values()` supplies the values in dictionary insertion order. Iterating a dictionary without a view supplies keys instead. A view reflects the mapping; it is not a detached snapshot.
entries.pitfall: A numeric total needs the stored quantities, not the string keys.

entries.title: Iterating keys, values and items
text: Iterating a dictionary directly gives keys. values supplies values; items supplies key/value pairs. Dictionaries preserve insertion order. Choose the view your calculation needs.
entries.pitfall: Do not add or remove keys while iterating that same dictionary. Build a separate result or plan the changes first.

entries.title: Counting occurrences with dictionaries
text: Use each distinct value as a key and its frequency as the mapped value. A missing-key default of zero supports one increment pattern for both new and repeated keys.
entries.pitfall: Normalize text only if the specification wants different spellings treated as the same key.

entries.title: Lists of records
text: A list can hold dictionaries with named fields. Iterate the list to choose a record, then use keys to read that record. The list controls order; the dictionary explains each field.
entries.pitfall: A shallow copy of the outer list still shares the dictionaries inside it.

entries.title: Remove a dictionary entry with `pop`
text: `mapping.pop(key, default)` removes and returns a value. A supplied default handles absence without insertion or deletion. `list.pop` uses positions; `dict.pop` uses keys.
entries.pitfall: An empty stored value is still present and must be returned faithfully.

entries.title: Insert values with f-strings
text: Put `f` before a quoted string and surround an expression with braces to include its value. The expression is evaluated when that string is built.
entries.code:
device = "Radio"
print(f"Ready: {device}")
entries.pitfall: Without the `f`, `{device}` is displayed as literal text.

entries.title: Find a wrong result
text: Code can run successfully and still calculate the wrong thing. Compare a small input and expected result with the actual output. Trace intermediate values to find the first disagreement.
entries.code:
length = 3
count = 4
print(length + count)  # 7, not the intended product 12
entries.pitfall: Changing the final message cannot repair a wrong calculation upstream.

entries.title: Parameters and arguments
text: A parameter is a name in a function definition. An argument supplies the value at a call. A caller name does not need to match the parameter name.
entries.code:
def double(value):
    return value * 2

amount = 6
print(double(amount))
entries.pitfall: A function object and a call are different: `double` names the function; `double(amount)` runs it.

entries.title: Keyword arguments
text: A keyword argument uses `parameter=value` inside a call. The keyword must match the definition. Naming arguments can make a call clearer when their meanings are easy to swap.
entries.pitfall: If you mix positional and keyword arguments, positional ones come first.

entries.title: Follow a result through helpers
text: A returned value can become an argument to another call. A named intermediate value makes the handoff easier to inspect. Read nested calls from the inside out.
entries.pitfall: Returning one value does not automatically pass it to the next function. The caller chooses where it goes.

entries.title: Local names during a call
text: Each call gives its parameters local bindings. Assigning a different integer to a local parameter does not reassign the caller name. `return` sends the value back across the boundary.
entries.code:
def plus_one(number):
    number = number + 1
    return number

original = 4
changed = plus_one(original)
entries.pitfall: Rebinding a name and mutating a shared list are different operations.

entries.title: The `pass` placeholder
text: `pass` does nothing. Use it when a syntactically required block is not implemented yet. A function with only `pass` reaches the end and returns `None`.
entries.pitfall: A `pass` is not a successful calculation; replace it with behavior that meets the contract.
